title: Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services

reading.body:
This incident shows impersonation at scale enabled by AI-generated media. Scammers created deepfake videos and fake social media profiles using the likeness of a real immigration attorney, then deployed these across multiple platforms to solicit payments for legal services the attorney never offered. The failure occurred in the moderation and verification systems of social media platforms, where thousands of fraudulent accounts remained active long enough to defraud vulnerable immigrants before being removed.

The scammers exploited the difficulty of distinguishing AI-generated impersonations from legitimate content, and they exploited the trust immigrants place in legal professionals offering services online. What would have caught this earlier: platform systems that verify the identity of users offering professional services, or systems that detect and flag deepfake video content before it accrues followers and victim reports.

It is not established how many people were defrauded, how the scammers obtained or generated the attorney's likeness, or what actions authorities have taken since the attorney's plan to contact them.

reports.title: Scammers steal identity of renowned Miami attorney to target immigrants on social media
South Florida immigration attorney says AI scammers are using his identity to target immigrants
Scammers use AI to impersonate immigration attorneys to dupe immigrants with fake legal services
Legal resident loses thousands seeking citizenship to AI immigration attorney

summary:
Angel Leal, a South Florida immigration attorney with over 30 years of experience, has become the target of artificial intelligence scammers who are using deepfake videos and fake social media profiles featuring his likeness to defraud vulnerable immigrants. The criminals are offering immigration services that Leal never provided, such as US residency assistance for undocumented immigrants without deportation orders, in exchange for payments ranging around $2,200. Leal first discovered the scheme when potential clients began calling his office, and the problem has escalated dramatically over the past three months.

To combat the fraud, Leal's firm hired an anti-piracy company that has successfully removed nearly 6,500 fake profiles across multiple platforms: 3,500 from TikTok, 2,400 from Facebook, and 544 from Instagram. The scammers typically direct victims through social media videos to WhatsApp numbers, where they send fake contracts and collect payments via money transfer apps like Venmo, Zelle, or Cash App. Leal plans to contact local and federal authorities this week to investigate the fraud and is warning immigrants to verify anyone offering legal services online and to avoid making payments through digital transfer services.
